newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge turns down Liggett injunction request.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge turns down Liggett injunction request.

text.p: A federal judge on Friday turned down a request by the Liggett Group Inc. tobacco firm for an injunction that would have blocked further legal actions and filings against the company.

Chief U.S. District Judge Charles Haden II said at a hearing that attorneys for Liggett and a plaintiff who suffers from lung cancer had not presented adequate evidence to support a court order that would have affected court cases across the United States.
Noting there are numerous tobacco lawsuits moving in courts across the nation, Haden said, "There is a race to the courthouse. A lot of economic interests are involved."
Attorneys for Liggett and the plaintiff, Earl William Walker Jr. of Poca, West Virginia, said they would bring more evidence to federal court to win the injunction.
The hearing for the injunction stemmed from a lawsuit filed in February against Liggett by Walker, who said 40 years of smoking Liggett cigarettes seriously damaged his health.
Walker was diagnosed with lung cancer last year.
James Humphreys, an attorney representing Walker, said he will bring in Liggett officers to testify about the company's financial health.

Although they are opponents in the case, Humphreys and Liggett attorney Michael Fay had asked Haden to issue the injunction to stop legal action that would have drained the cigarette maker's finances.
Fay said Liggett is in "a precarious financial condition," but Haden said there had been no testimony from witnesses with knowledge about the case and about Liggett's financial condition.
Haden said the case will remain open for attorneys to present further evidence. No date was scheduled for a second hearing.
Haden on Friday also allowed 11 states to drop out of the case after they argued they had involuntarily been added as plaintiffs.
Several of those states said they already are in negotiations with tobacco companies in other court cases and they said the West Virginia federal case might jeopardize those talks.
